item.title: Pickleball in China: How a tiny ball is driving a big industry
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-14
Pickleball, a sport originating in the United States and combining elements of tennis, badminton and table tennis, is gaining popularity across China, bringing new opportunities to cities and creating another platform for sporting exchanges between China and the rest of the world. ZHENGZHOU, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 China National Pickleball Championships was held in early September in Hebi, central China's Henan Province, drawing more than 30 teams from across the country. Preliminary statistics show that pickleball, once a niche sport, has been included as a mass-participation event in the games of 10 provincial-level regions this year, including Henan, Guangxi and Beijing. The China Pickleball Circuit, which had just over 80 stops when it launched in 2024, has expanded to 1,000 stops this year. Originating in the United States and combining elements of tennis, badminton and table tennis, pickleball is rapidly gaining popularity across China. The sport is bringing new opportunities to cities and creating another platform for sporting exchanges between China and the rest of the world. A CITY TRANSFORMED BY A BALL Every morning, the sharp crack of pickleballs echoes along the banks of the Qi River in Hebi. Zhang Shaohua, a Hebi resident born in the 1970s, has been hooked on pickleball since she first tried it in 2024. To promote the sport more widely, she set up a players' community and built her own professional pickleball venue. She also travels regularly around the country to play and connect with other enthusiasts. "In Hebi, pickleball started as a trend, but it has become a daily routine," Zhang said. In just three years, the once-obscure sport has taken off in Hebi. "Hebi has a solid industrial foundation and rich cultural and tourism resources, but its urban visibility and influence still need to be enhanced. We urgently need to build a highly recognizable city brand that can connect with both domestic and international markets," said Zhao Hongyu, secretary of the CPC Hebi Municipal Committee. By 2025, the city had built 1,600 pickleball courts, giving it one of the highest densities of pickleball courts in China and forming a network covering urban areas, counties and townships. Pickleball has not only raised Hebi's profile, but also helped spur the development of related industries. Leveraging its existing coal chemical, rubber and plastics industries, Hebi has built a pickleball industrial chain that spans from raw materials such as polypropylene to the production of high-end equipment. At a factory in Xun County, Hebi, machines hum as pickleball paddles, nets and sports flooring roll off the production line. The company, which started as a rubber and plastic products manufacturer, began making pickleball equipment in 2024. Its pickleball equipment sales exceeded 25 million yuan in 2025, up more than 50 percent year on year, and are projected to top 50 million yuan in 2026. "We export pickleball-related products to Europe, the Americas and Southeast Asia," said Xing Weimin, general manager of Henan Geli Sports Goods Co., Ltd. "Recently, customers have come to the factory almost every day to discuss business. The pickleball market has huge potential." A SPORT SPREADING WIDELY IN CHINA In 2026, pickleball is surging across China with unprecedented momentum, sweeping through cities large and small and drawing participants from schoolchildren to retirees alike. "There are currently eight million people in China who regularly participate in pickleball, and about 20 million who have tried it," said Bai Xilin, director of the Tennis Administration Center of China's General Administration of Sport. "The number of active pickleball players in China may reach 30 million in the future." Beyond Hebi, cities across China are exploring creative ways to weave pickleball into urban life. Hangzhou's Gongshu District has turned unused space beneath an elevated highway into a 6,000-square-meter pickleball park with five standard courts. Beijing's Fengtai District has converted a former indoor basketball arena into a pickleball club that now hosts the Beijing Pickleball Super League. Suzhou, Jiangsu Province, has opened a 23-court complex, the largest in the province, which offered four hours of play for just 29.9 yuan during the summer, drawing scores of young players. Nanjing has 11 standard courts on the 51st floor of a shopping mall, offering panoramic city views. Hosting pickleball tournaments has also emerged as a new way to blend culture, sports, tourism and commerce while stimulating local consumption. "I believe that pickleball has the potential to become the next marathon-like popular sport," said Song Hongfei, general manager of the sports business division at Viva Goods Co., Ltd. According to the China Sporting Goods Federation, China's domestic market for pickleball equipment and services exceeded 1.8 billion yuan in 2025 and is projected to grow at a compound annual rate of 47 percent over the next five years. Enthusiasm for hosting tournaments is also surging. In just over two years, China Pickleball Circuit events alone have been staged in 99 cities across more than 20 provincial-level regions, while grassroots tournaments have proliferated as well. "Many cities host marathons, which not only promote national fitness but also play an important role in enhancing the city's brand, and pickleball is developing in the same direction," said Qiao Liang of Henan Dongcheng Sports Industry Co., Ltd. MORE THAN JUST A GAME Bai Xilin described pickleball's broad appeal as "three lows and three highs." The "three lows" start with a low barrier to entry: men and women, young and old, and even complete beginners can pick it up quickly. Second is low cost-courts are flexible and equipment is relatively inexpensive. Third is low risk: as a non-contact sport, it suits a wide range of ages. The "three highs" are its strong social dimension, high overall value and high safety rating. Its overall value encompasses fitness, social, economic and cultural benefits. Pickleball has also seen rapid international growth in recent years. According to 2026 statistics from a sports and fitness industry association in the United States, where the sport originated, pickleball has been the fastest-growing sport in the country for five consecutive years. In Southeast Asia, including Vietnam and the Philippines, it has also built a broad participation base. In 2025, the Hebi International Pickleball Invitational brought together professional players from 14 countries and regions, including Spain, Italy and Sweden, to compete alongside Chinese athletes and exchange skills. In February and August this year, two groups of American teachers and students visited Hebi. They paired up with local teenagers for friendly matches and shared pickleball skills. They also visited an ancient temple fair, experienced a molten-iron fireworks display and made traditional clay whistles known as "Nigugu," gaining deeper insight into Chinese culture. Through friendly matches and cultural exchanges, pickleball is creating lasting bonds that transcend borders and bring people closer together. ■

item.title: In Yan'an, visitors see how CPC turns history into progress
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-14
YAN'AN, Shaanxi, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- When Ivan Racan was still a boy, not yet 10 years old, his father returned to Croatia from China in 1981, carrying with him a sanxian -- a traditional three-stringed Chinese instrument. The instrument hung on the wall of his childhood room, bringing a piece of distant China into his everyday life. More than 40 years later, Racan came across a similar instrument at a museum in Shanghai. He was struck by the realization that while the sanxian had remained much the same, China itself had transformed dramatically. For Racan, a member of the Croatian Parliament and son of former Croatian Prime Minister Ivica Racan, the instrument connects two periods of China's modern history. His father had visited China as an official of the former Yugoslavia. When he returned, he brought back stories that captured the early days of a transformation, one that would go on to reshape the country over the decades to come, Racan said. Decades later, Racan visited China himself and made a point to travel to Yan'an, which was once a center of the Chinese revolution. During his journey through the city in northwest China's Shaanxi Province, he encountered a modern country that would have been difficult to imagine in 1981. On Sept. 10, more than 200 representatives from over 50 countries attended a thematic briefing in Yan'an. Through stories of rural development, ecological conservation, industrial upgrading and cultural heritage protection, the event demonstrated how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has translated long-term goals into changes that reach communities and ordinary families. "This is something that has to be commended, appreciated, studied," Racan told Xinhua. For Petre Danci, a parliamentary advisor at the Office of the Secretary of the Romanian Senate and secretary of the Romania-China Friendship Group within the Alliance for the Union of Romanians, China's transformation is not an inherited memory. It is part of his own life. Danci, who speaks fluent Mandarin, arrived in Beijing in 2011. He studied Chinese at the Capital University of Economics and Business before completing bachelor's and master's degrees. During seven years of study and life in Beijing, he experienced China through lectures, friendships and the everyday norms of student life. "Every single time I come to China, I see a lot of development," he said. "Even if I go to a very familiar city, like Beijing, or Shanghai, or some other big cities, I still see the improvement." His latest journey to Yan'an brought him face to face with an earlier chapter of China's history. Danci learned about the period when Yan'an served as a center of the Chinese revolution and said he could still feel the Yan'an spirit in China today. That connection became clearer when he heard about the development of Liangjiahe Village, the technological upgrading of traditional industries and the restoration of environmentally fragile land through years of afforestation. "It takes function, leadership and organization," Danci told Xinhua. He believed China's experience in agriculture, ecological restoration and industrial modernization could offer useful references for Romania. Such experience should not be copied mechanically, he said, but adapted to local conditions through exchanges among people, businesses and governments. Having studied the Chinese language and experienced the country as a student, Danci said he hoped to help strengthen communication between Romania and China. The connection between Yan'an's revolutionary history and China's present-day development was expressed most directly by Leevameng Leebouapao, deputy director general of the Land Department at the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment of Laos. During a visit to Nangou Village in Yan'an, he saw how poverty alleviation, public infrastructure and improvements to the rural environment had changed people's lives. "Socialism creates conditions for equality," he said. "People have equal access to education, healthcare, transport and other public services. China has demonstrated this in practice." What impressed him was that development had not been limited to major cities such as Beijing and Shanghai. Roads, communications networks and public services had also reached rural communities. In Nangou Village, he said, the practical work of the CPC and the government had made life more convenient for villagers and significantly improved their living environment. He added that China's experience in poverty alleviation and improving people's livelihoods deserved to be studied by other developing countries, including Laos. Beneath Pagoda Hill in Yan'an, visitors did not simply listen to stories about the CPC's past, but also to how the spirit formed in Yan'an continues to shape China's development today. ■

item.title: Southern Europe shows renewed economic resilience amid eurozone slowdown
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-14
* Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece, all deeply affected by Europe's sovereign debt crisis over a decade ago, have shown renewed vitality and resilience in recent years. * Southern Europe's service-heavy economies and growing use of renewable energy had made them less vulnerable to some of the energy and trade shocks weighing on Europe's industrial core. * The IMF's 2025 Regional Economic Outlook urged Europe to accelerate structural reforms while keeping trade open. Southern European countries have sought to combine the two, building on post-crisis reforms and existing industrial strengths while pursuing trade and investment ties with emerging economies. * China has played a constructive role in this process through trade, investment and industrial partnerships. MADRID, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- As the eurozone faces a subdued growth outlook, a different economic picture has emerged along its southern flank: Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece, all deeply affected by Europe's sovereign debt crisis over a decade ago, have shown renewed vitality and resilience in recent years. In the second quarter of 2026, seasonally adjusted GDP in the euro area increased by 1.0 percent year-on-year. In contrast, Spain, Portugal and Greece recorded growth of 2.7 percent, 2.5 percent and 1.9 percent, respectively, while Italy matched the eurozone rate. A report published in June by Allianz, an insurance company, described Southern Europe's post-2021 performance as "a clear shift in the geography of Eurozone growth, with Southern economies moving from chronic underperformance to cyclical leadership." Analysts and market observers attribute this resilience to three overlapping shifts: a broader mix of growth drivers, financial and institutional repair reinforced by EU investment, and a pragmatic openness to external markets, capital and technology, including expanding industrial partnerships with China. Together, these factors have helped Southern Europe withstand some of the pressures weighing on the eurozone's traditional industrial core. SHOCKS SHIFTED SIDES Recent shocks -- from supply-chain disruptions to energy-price spikes and trade tensions -- have not fallen evenly across the eurozone. "In the current cycle, the asymmetry of external shocks has, so to speak, shifted sides," Pablo Sanz, a professor at Spain's National University of Distance Education, said in an interview with Xinhua. Sanz said Southern Europe's service-heavy economies and growing use of renewable energy had made them less vulnerable to some of the energy and trade shocks weighing on Europe's industrial core. The difference is also visible in the drivers of growth. In the second quarter of 2026, Spain's economy ministry said growth was supported by domestic demand, investment and industry, while Portugal's rebound was driven mainly by net external demand. Investment, construction and services have supported Italy in recent years, while investment, consumption and net exports all contributed to Greece's growth in 2025. Tourism also remains an important source of activity, employment and services exports, particularly in Spain, Portugal and Greece. A changing energy mix has provided another buffer. Eurostat data showed that over 60 percent of gross electricity consumption in Portugal, Greece and Spain came from renewable sources in 2025. The European Commission said growing renewable generation had lowered wholesale electricity prices, with gas influencing prices in only a minority of market hours in the Iberian Peninsula. Labor supply has provided further support, particularly in Spain. According to Sanz, labor-market reforms that reduced excessive reliance on temporary contracts helped stabilize household incomes, while immigration expanded the workforce and supported employment and domestic demand. Public investment has added another leg to the recovery. Allianz estimates that Italy, Spain, Portugal and Greece together account for almost 60 percent of funding under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), the centerpiece of NextGenerationEU. "Public capital injected through NextGenerationEU funds has therefore served as a countercyclical firewall, financing green-transition infrastructure, digitalization and key industrial projects without placing excessive strain on national finances," Sanz said. REFORM DIVIDENDS The recent divergence also reflects differences in the timing of adjustment. The sovereign debt crisis forced Southern Europe to confront long-standing financial and structural imbalances. The process varied across countries. Greece and Portugal entered broad assistance programs covering fiscal consolidation, bank repair, pension reform, and changes to labor and product markets. Spain received assistance focused on its banking sector, while Italy remained outside a bailout program and followed a more gradual course. The adjustment carried a high economic and social cost, as domestic demand contracted and unemployment surged. Over time, however, banks reduced non-performing loans, households and businesses cut debt, and labor- and product-market rules were revised. Spain and Portugal also broke with a pattern of running external deficits during periods of expansion and began regularly recording current-account surpluses. A 2026 study by the National Bank of Belgium found that Spain, Portugal and Greece grew at an average annual rate of 1.7 percent between 2019 and 2025, compared with 0.6 percent for Germany, France, the Netherlands and Belgium. It linked their stronger performance partly to post-crisis reforms and fiscal consolidation. Greece shows how the repair extended to the functioning of public institutions. According to the IMF, measures targeting tax evasion and informality helped narrow its value-added tax compliance gap from 24 percent in 2019 to about 9 percent in 2024. Reforms have also covered the judiciary, business regulation and tax administration, although weak productivity and judicial delays remain constraints. After the pandemic, EU conditionality took a different form. Rather than focusing primarily on correcting imbalances, RRF funding was tied to national recovery and resilience plans combining investment projects with reform commitments, with at least 37 percent of the budget allocated to climate and biodiversity and a further minimum of 20 percent to digital measures. The plans have directed funding toward renewable energy, power grids, sustainable transport, industrial decarbonization and digitalization. According to Sanz, Spain and Portugal have used EU funding for electric-vehicle value chains, industrial decarbonization and the digitalization of public administrations and small businesses, while Italy has coupled investment with reforms of public administration, the justice system and public procurement. However, these gains should not be overstated. Sanz cautioned that, except in some technological and renewable-energy niches, Southern Europe's productivity gap with Northern Europe remained substantial. An analysis published by the Jacques Delors Institute noted that the four countries entered the pandemic on different growth trajectories and have deployed RRF funds at different speeds. Although the facility has supported demand and investment, the analysis said, its lasting impact will depend on whether the projects and reforms raise productivity and potential growth. The IMF's 2025 Regional Economic Outlook urged Europe to accelerate structural reforms while keeping trade open. Southern European countries have sought to combine the two, building on post-crisis reforms and existing industrial strengths while pursuing trade and investment ties with emerging economies. COOPERATION WITH CHINA China has played a constructive role in this process through trade, investment and industrial partnerships. In Spain, cooperation with Chinese companies is increasingly moving beyond trade toward local manufacturing in the electric-mobility supply chain. Chery's partnership with Spanish automaker Ebro has revived production at the former Nissan plant in Barcelona, while CATL and Stellantis are jointly investing in a lithium iron phosphate battery plant in Zaragoza. "Spain has become a gateway not only for distribution but also for manufacturing, taking advantage of the auto manufacturing ecosystem that our country has," said Raul Morales, communications director at Faconauto, Spain's federation of automotive dealers' associations, in an interview with Xinhua. Portugal is following a similar pattern. Chinese battery manufacturer CALB is developing its first European factory in the Sines Industrial and Logistics Zone. The 2 billion-euro project is expected to create 1,800 direct jobs and help Portugal develop a battery value chain around its lithium resources. In Greece, China COSCO Shipping Corporation (COSCO) acquired a majority stake in Piraeus Port Authority in 2016, becoming the operator of the entire port. The port has since strengthened its position as a major Mediterranean container hub. Stefanos Gkikas, Greek deputy minister of maritime affairs and insular policy, described the cooperation between COSCO and the port authority as "productive," saying it had enhanced the port's competitiveness and strengthened Greece's position in global shipping. In Italy, the Ministry of Enterprises and Made in Italy, Italian renewable-energy developer Renexia and China's MingYang Smart Energy have agreed to work toward establishing wind-turbine manufacturing capacity. The proposed investment, worth around 500 million euros (579.2 million U.S. dollars), is linked to the planned 2.8-GW Med Wind floating offshore wind project off Sicily. Sanz described the four countries' approach to China as "a form of reasonable industrial pragmatism aligned with their growth needs." "Greater openness to emerging economies is an undeniable advantage for Southern Europe's economic dynamism, provided that it takes the form of co-investment, technology transfer and local job creation," he said. "The success of Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece will therefore depend on their ability to manage the complex balance between attracting highly competitive global capital and complying with EU regulations," he added. ■

item.title: Smart technologies power high-quality development of China's mining industry
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-14
TIANJIN, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- At the exhibition booth of Unissky (Nanjing) Technology Co., Ltd., a four-legged inspection robot moved steadily, autonomously adjusting its movements when encountering obstacles and following predefined routes. Designed for inspection in confined and hazardous spaces such as underground mines, the robot drew the attention of many visitors to the 2026 China Mining Conference and Exhibition. "This product is primarily designed for confined and hazardous environments such as underground mines, and it has broad application potential in the mining sector," said Xu Tao, a solution manager at Unissky. The global mining industry is undergoing a profound digital transformation. In recent years, China has embraced smart technologies to modernize its mining industry, with digital twins, autonomous mining, and AI-powered exploration gaining ground across operations. China's push for smart mining is helping drive the industry into a new stage of development. The coal industry offers a glimpse of this transformation. By the end of 2025, China had 1,066 intelligent coal mines, with intelligent production capacity accounting for more than 65 percent of total coal production capacity, according to data from the China National Coal Association. Artificial intelligence is being rapidly adopted across the coal industry, with applications spanning production and operations, safety management, and equipment maintenance. Autonomous driving technology is also gaining ground in open-pit mines. In China, more than 4,000 autonomous mining trucks were in operation by the end of 2025, according to industry statistics. In 2024, seven Chinese government departments jointly issued the guiding opinions on advancing the construction of intelligent mines and promoting the safe development of mines. The document calls for establishing a comprehensive system covering technology, equipment and management for smart mining by 2030, with greater integration and broader sharing of mining data. Ren Shoumai, an official at the China Geological Survey, said geological mapping is like drawing a "geological navigation map" for the subsurface mineral world. On Friday, the Ministry of Natural Resources unveiled an AI-powered mineral exploration system, AI-OreSeeking, and an AI-powered geological mapping system, AI-GeoMapping, aiming to reshape geological survey workflows and provide a new technological paradigm for global mineral exploration. AI-GeoMapping has been widely trialed on nearly 100 1:50,000-scale geological map sheets in Qinghai, Xizang, Xinjiang, Fujian, and other provincial-level regions of China, and has also been promoted in Morocco, Saudi Arabia, Laos and other countries. It identifies geological bodies with overall accuracy exceeding 90 percent and improves the efficiency of data processing, integrated analysis and geological map compilation by more than 50 percent compared with traditional methods. Experts attending the event said cutting-edge technologies such as artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things and 5G have become increasingly integrated into the entire mining lifecycle, driving breakthroughs in areas such as smart mine development and mining machinery manufacturing. At Huangling Mining Co., Ltd., a subsidiary of Shaanxi Coal and Chemical Industry Group, production data at the No. 1 Coal Mine are updated in milliseconds on screens at the surface dispatch and command center. Folds in rock layers and variations in coal seam thickness that were previously difficult to observe are now converted into 3D visual data through smart technologies, enabling more precise prediction and dynamic control of underground operations. At Yidong Group's Lijiata Coal Mine, a high-precision personnel positioning system and a 5G-based communication and dispatch system have created an underground high-speed information network, significantly improving mine safety management and emergency response. At Qinglong Coal Mine, operated by Guizhou Qianxi Energy Development Co., Ltd., intelligent shearers equipped with memory cutting and automatic following, as well as intelligent roadheaders featuring inertial navigation, laser positioning and infrared remote control, are being used in mining operations. These technologies have significantly reduced the physical workload of workers while boosting production efficiency. "Mining robots are helping enable unmanned operation at fixed workstations and robotic operations at hazardous posts," said Wang Lin, a marketing manager at CITIC HIC Kaicheng Intelligence Equipment Co., Ltd. The company's coal-gangue sorting robot on display at the conference uses big-data-based intelligent recognition technology to automatically identify and separate coal from gangue, helping mining companies improve sorting efficiency and operating returns, Wang said. Smart mining practices are also being extended to other fields. During the construction of a reservoir bridge in Macheng, central China's Hubei Province, the project team of China Railway 18th Bureau Group Co., Ltd. applied smart technologies to key construction processes and independently developed a range of tools, including a precision positioning device for embedded sleeves in track slabs. These innovations have helped address long-standing challenges such as significant positioning deviations in traditional manual operations, significantly improving construction quality and precision. Wang Sufeng, deputy director and secretary-general of the Smart Mine Professional Committee of the China Association of Work Safety, said smart mining is key to developing new quality productive forces and enhancing workplace safety, and is an essential path to the industry's high-quality development. Looking ahead, experts said the industry needs to improve intelligent decision-making and inter-system coordination, build centralized data platforms to enable data sharing, and accelerate the development of technologies for transparent geological information and safer, more energy-efficient power systems. Industry insiders called for closer cooperation among government agencies, mining companies, equipment manufacturers, universities and research institutes to advance smart mining and inject new momentum into the industry's high-quality development. ■

item.title: Fueling Japan's neo-militarism will push region toward dangerous vortex: Chinese spokesperson
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-14
BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese defense spokesperson on Monday voiced firm opposition to a joint military exercise by Japan, the United States and Australia, warning that moves promoting Japan's military ambitions will drive the region into a perilous vortex. Jiang Bin, a spokesperson for the Ministry of National Defense, made the remarks at a press briefing when responding to a query concerning the "Orient Shield 26" exercise, which is being held in Japan from Sept. 8 to 24. This exercise is packaged as a "shield," but in reality it amounts to the forward deployment of strategic offensive weapons. It not only undermines other countries' legitimate security interests, but also heightens the risk of an arms race and military confrontation, and seriously threatens regional security and stability, Jiang said. Japan, as a defeated country of World War II, is prohibited from obtaining offensive weapons by the Potsdam Proclamation and Japan's pacifist constitution itself. However, in recent years, the country has continuously broken the constraints and its exclusively defense-oriented policy, vigorously developed long-range offensive weapons, and leveraged joint exercises with foreign countries to accelerate its "remilitarization," the spokesperson noted. "Any move that fuels Japan's military ambitions will only push the region into a dangerous vortex and will inevitably bring harm to those involved," Jiang warned. China urges relevant countries to respect other nations' security concerns, correct their wrong practices, and play a positive role in regional peace and stability with concrete actions, Jiang added. ■

item.title: China's yuan loans increase by 10.44 trln yuan in Jan.-Aug. period
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-14
BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's yuan-denominated loans rose by 10.44 trillion yuan (about 1.54 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first eight months of 2026, central bank data showed on Monday. At the end of August, outstanding yuan loans stood at 282.35 trillion yuan, up 4.9 percent year on year, according to the People's Bank of China. M2, a broad measure of money supply that covers cash in circulation and all deposits, had increased by 7.5 percent year on year to 356.81 trillion yuan by the end of last month. M1, which covers currency in circulation, corporate demand deposits, personal demand deposits and provisions received by non-bank payment institutions, reached 115.77 trillion yuan at the end of August, a rise of 4.1 percent from a year earlier. China's outstanding aggregate financing to the real economy stood at 464.8 trillion yuan at the end of August, up 7.2 percent year on year, the central bank noted. "At present, China's aggregate financial volume is growing at a reasonable pace, and social financing conditions have remained relatively loose," said Tian Xuan, dean of Peking University's Guanghua School of Management. The central bank said in its latest monetary policy report that it will continue to implement a moderately loose monetary policy in the second half of 2026, strengthen counter-cyclical adjustment, and take solid steps to promote sustained and improved economic development. It will also maintain ample liquidity, guide financial institutions to enhance the balance of credit supply, and align the growth of social financing and money supply with expected targets for economic growth and overall price levels. Wang Qing, chief macro analyst at Golden Credit Rating, said that looking ahead, the country's monetary policy will strengthen coordination with fiscal and industrial policies and step up counter-cyclical adjustment. Structural monetary policy tools are expected to see further price cuts, increased quotas and expanded coverage, to boost financing support for tech companies and private enterprises, facilitate the shift to new growth drivers, and stabilize overall employment, Wang said. ■

item.title: China's smart home consumption push moves beyond individual devices
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-14
BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- For 72-year-old Zhu Chengyi and his wife Li Lan, 71, replacing a decade-old air conditioner in their home in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, brought more than just cooler air. Their new smart air conditioner can respond to voice commands and be controlled through a mobile app, allowing their daughter living in Guangdong Province, also in south China, to help adjust the temperature remotely. The couple made this upgrade under China's consumer goods trade-in program, as the country's smart home market increasingly moves beyond individual appliance upgrades toward more connected household systems. China on Monday unveiled an action plan to further promote smart home consumption by enriching application scenarios and expanding high-quality supply. The plan, jointly issued by eight government departments including the Ministry of Commerce, the National Development and Reform Commission and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, also calls for supporting elderly-friendly renovation and smart upgrading of older homes while better meeting the consumption needs of different groups. The plan sets out seven measures to expand high-quality smart home supply, improve the smart home standards system, support smart home consumption, develop elderly-friendly smart home products, streamline the service chain for recycling used household goods, optimize community services, and strengthen fiscal and financial support. The plan comes as Chinese consumers are increasingly looking beyond simple product replacement toward broader upgrades in home living. Chinese consumers are shifting from meeting basic needs to pursuing quality experiences and from simple product replacement to holistic lifestyle upgrades, according to a white paper released by the China Household Electrical Appliances Association earlier this year. It identified major trends for 2026, including a shift from passive response to proactive intelligence, deeper integration of health-related scenarios, the robotization of home appliances, and the development of whole-home artificial intelligence ecosystems. To expand supply, the plan encourages manufacturers to step up research and development of smart home products, and supports home furnishing stores and shopping malls in setting up smart home experience centers and model rooms for whole-home smart systems and digital homes. Regarding standards, it calls for improving the grading and evaluation standards system for smart home products, and accelerating the formulation and implementation of mandatory national standards on connectivity and interoperability. To support consumption, the plan encourages local authorities to determine eligible smart home product categories and subsidy standards based on local conditions under China's 2026 consumer goods trade-in policy. Under this policy, local governments have greater flexibility in designing subsidy programs. The country plans to allocate 250 billion yuan (about 36.93 billion U.S. dollars) in ultra-long special treasury bond funds to support the nationwide program. China's consumer trade-in programs generated 1.1 trillion yuan in sales in the first half of 2026, benefiting consumers on 150 million occasions, with home appliance trade-ins reaching 63.27 million units and purchases of digital and smart products totaling 79.1 million units. The plan encourages home furnishing and decoration businesses to work with recycling companies to combine the delivery of new products with the collection of used ones. At the community level, the plan supports the establishment of home renovation service stations to provide services such as maintenance, storage, recycling and replacement. The plan also encourages financial institutions to diversify consumer finance products and services and expand lending for smart-home consumption, including by leveraging the country's interest-subsidy policy for personal consumption loans. For elderly consumers, the plan promotes home service robots, health monitoring and smart care products, and encourages elderly-friendly design in areas like ease of operation, dialect recognition and safety. Such products are already finding their way into Chinese homes. A home service robot developer at the 2026 World Robot Conference said its robots were already in paid use in more than 500 households, performing tasks such as basic housework, family companionship and pet care. Other robots are being developed specifically for elderly care, with functions ranging from companionship and mobility assistance to recording health data, including blood pressure and blood glucose levels. A report by the China Software Testing Center projected that China's elderly-care service robot market will exceed 10 billion yuan in 2026. Such applications form part of a broader push to upgrade smart home consumption, which is in line with China's plan for expanding consumption during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The plan calls for smart upgrades to home appliances and furnishings, better connectivity among smart home devices, and a shift from smart individual products toward whole-home smart systems. ■

item.title: China to create more friendly environment for childbearing with better childcare services
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-14
The State Council Information Office holds a press conference on making decisive progress in the Healthy China initiative in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Yuwei) BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- China will take further steps to support childbearing, including making childcare more accessible and affordable, a senior health official announced Monday, as the country seeks to ease costs of raising children and boost its birth rate. Lei Haichao, head of the National Health Commission, told a media conference that continuous efforts will be made to promote the integrated development of services at kindergartens and nursery centers and to support communities and employers in setting up childcare facilities. The aim is to ensure that families can access childcare services close to their homes or workplaces and at relatively affordable prices, Lei said. The commission will work to raise coverage of childcare services among young children to effectively reduce families' costs of having, raising and educating children, the official said. The country will also work to improve access to pediatric care at grassroots medical institutions, according to Lei. By the end of this year, 1,000 more community-level medical and health institutions will be capable of offering pediatric care compared with last year, Lei said, adding that by that time, more than 95 percent of the country's township-level clinics and community health service centers are expected to have the capacity to provide relevant services. Over 3,000 pediatricians have been sent from higher-level hospitals to grassroots medical institutions to strengthen pediatric services at the community level, Lei said. China has developed a full-cycle maternity support system covering pre-pregnancy, pregnancy and childbirth, and child-rearing, with measures that include maternity allowances, childcare subsidies, medical insurance reimbursement and affordable childcare services to ease the financial burden on families with children. The country introduced a nationwide childcare subsidy program in 2025, offering an annual tax-free subsidy of 3,600 yuan (about 530 U.S. dollars) for each child under the age of three. It also began waiving childcare and education fees for the final year of kindergarten in the 2025 autumn semester. As of August, more than 25 million infants and toddlers have received childcare subsidies for 2026, and about 24 million children enrolled in kindergartens have benefited from the fee-waiving policy. Also, 260 million people are currently covered by maternity insurance, and many regions are expanding coverage to allow flexible workers to enroll in maternity insurance alongside employee medical insurance. These policies are among China's broader efforts to build a birth-friendly society amid declining birth rates and an aging population. Building a "birth-friendly society" has become a key focus of China's 15th Five-Year Plan. The outline sets out measures, including incentives to encourage births and efforts to reduce the costs of childbirth, childcare and education. It says the goal is to stabilize the number of newborns and support long-term balanced population development. ■
